newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Punt jumps as election revives revaluation rumours.
newsitem.headline: Punt jumps as election revives revaluation rumours.

text.p: The Irish pound jumped by nearly a penny against sterling and by two pfennigs against the mark in morning trade on Monday as the prospect of a new Irish government revived revaluation rumours, dealers said.

"There are rumours of the Irish pound being revalued and that's caused something of a short squeeze," one dealer said. "But the market is pretty illiquid and it doesn't take much to move it at the moment."

The centre-right opposition of Fianna Fail and the Progressive Democrats won 81 out of 166 parliamentary seats in Friday's elections, defeating the centre-left "Rainbow Coalition" of Prime Minister John Bruton.
Although they are two seats short of an overall majority, analysts say support from a number of sympathetic Independents should allow them to form a new government.

Economists said there should be no real change to the broad thrust of Irish macro-economic policy but the prospect of a new government fuelled market talk of a revaluation to stop recent selling of the punt on the belief it would enter EMU at a rate well below current levels against the mark.
By 1000 GMT, the Irish pound was at 0.9215 sterling against 0.9130 at Friday's close. It rose to 2.5905 marks from 2.5705 last week.
Dealers said talk of a delay to European economic and monetary union (EMU) may also have bolstered the Irish pound.

"If EMU was delayed, the convergence plays with the Irish pound going back toward its ERM central parity would be gone and the movement toward 2.41 marks is put on a very long finger," one trader noted.
Attention is now focused on the Ecofin meeting in Luxembourg as the market waits to hear France's views on the post-EMU budget stability pact.
Dealers said that aside from reviving revaluation rumours, Friday's Irish election had little impact on the market.

"If anything, the election would be a marginal negative if it was important at all but it's not," one trader said. "You're going to have a minority government where you are relying on a couple of Independents which is not the ideal situation but it's not really a factor in the market."
